prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: I keep B022 as my preferred configuration, but with less confidence than in round 1, and I want to say exactly why. The prize would rest on two things that are no longer in dispute: a quantitative continuum-model prediction that bands flatten near 1.1 degrees (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011), and the 2018 experimental demonstration, by Jarillo-Herrero's group, that at that angle a single tunable carbon system hosts correlated insulators and superconductivity. The twist angle is a clean control parameter, and the observations have since been reproduced by many groups and carried to other platforms such as twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides. That is the pattern of a sharp prediction followed by an unexpected experiment, which I weigh heavily. The citation does not need a theory of the superconductivity; it honours flat-band-driven correlated phases, which are established. The three names map onto the prediction and the discovery without inventing a fourth contributor.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my own choice is the one Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce and Kroll press, and I now find it stronger than I did a round ago: the pairing mechanism and several correlated states are unsettled eight years on, twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample reproducibility, and Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive papers, is outside the three names. The statutes cap the prize at three, so I cannot repair that, and the citation would have to say openly that it honours the prediction and the discovery and not every contributor. B036 has a stable interpretation, independent confirmation across Sr, Yb and Hg, and a two-name credit that maps onto two identifiable contributions. If the committee judges that an unrepaired credit gap and unsettled interpretation outweigh breadth of impact, B036 is the right prize this year and I would vote for it without reluctance.

responses.point: In round 1 you argued that the magic-wavelength lattice is a conceptual step distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and that maturity is decisive for B036 this year.
responses.response: This moved me on the overlap question. I had ranked B036 fourth largely because of the comb and ion-control lineage. Your point that neither prior prize contains the idea of trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, so that light shifts cancel on the clock transition, is a real conceptual step and not an engineering refinement, and it is what lets the clock average over many atoms. I withdraw the overlap as my main objection. What remains between us is the weighing of precision against a new phenomenon, and the unresolved credit for Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto. Where we still differ is the maturity criterion: I think replication across many groups and materials gives a robust phenomenology even while the mechanism is open, so I do not treat that as decisive against B022.

responses.point: You describe the clock result as another digit of precision and not a new phenomenon, but still prefer it because the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the result, not its justification, and you argue B022 would reward a field whose central interpretation is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second should play no role in our decision, and that improves the case for B036 on its own terms. I disagree with the unsettled-interpretation framing: the interpretation that is unsettled is the superconducting pairing, while what a citation would credit, flat bands at the magic angle and the correlated insulator and superconducting states observed there, is reproduced. I accept your point that Cao's absence is a real fairness cost, and I would not word the citation to suggest otherwise. Your own ranking of B022 as an alternative suggests we differ on timing and not on merit, which I find a narrower disagreement than the ballots suggest.

responses.point: You keep B022 first and say you would accept a precision-measurement prize but would not put it above a genuine opening of a new field.
responses.response: I share the reading of the discovery, and I agree the SI redefinition adds no scientific weight. I would be more cautious than you about how far a new field outweighs maturity: the chair asks whether we would accept B036 if the Cao credit gap is judged unrepaired, and my answer is yes. I would accept it, because a three-name cap that omits the first author of the decisive experiments is a real cost, not a footnote. I do not think the omission disqualifies B022, but if the committee finds it does, I would not hold the prize hostage to my first choice.

responses.point: You argue that B022 leaves out the person who did the decisive measurement and so invites a credit controversy that B036 does not, and that the chair sees no clean two-part pairing with B036.
responses.response: The credit comparison is fair and I conceded it above. On the two-part question I looked at it carefully: every B022 configuration needs all three names, and B036 needs two, so no pairing with B022 fits inside three people, and a split with my other alternatives is not viable either. I therefore propose a single part. Where I would push back is the claim that the controversy attaches only to B022. Any prize for B036 still leaves out Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the national-laboratory groups, as you note yourself, so the difference is of degree. I accept that it is a difference of degree in B036's favour.

responses.point: You defend B054 against the 2016 overlap by reading the earlier citation as about topological phase transitions with broken time-reversal symmetry, and you accept the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap cannot be repaired.
responses.response: Your reading of 2016 is a fair distinction and I concede that overlap is weaker than I suggested in round 1. But the credit gap you accept remains decisive for me: the HgTe prediction that made the experiment possible comes from people outside the three names, and one of them is deceased, so the gap is permanent. In B022 the prediction and the experiment come from the credited names themselves, and the gap is the first author, which is also a real gap. Given that both have gaps, I would treat B054 as an alternative for your colleagues and not as a ranking above B022 or B036 for me.

responses.point: You ask the experimentalists how decisive the experimental side of jamming is, and you note that I am the only member who ranked B034 at all.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and it has not been answered by anyone, including me. The scaling picture at the jamming point is stable and numerically well tested, but the experimental landmark and the relation to glass physics are not yet something I can cite as a single decisive result, so I do not push B034. The cited result would be the identification of the isostatic point and its critical scaling, and I cannot defend that as a prize-ready discovery with only my ballot behind it. I therefore replace B034 with B046 as my second alternative. Your B046 trio of Zoller, Bloch and Greiner is one I could support, and its main cost, the exclusion of Cirac, Esslinger and Jaksch, is yours to answer.

uncertainties: Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism and sample-to-sample twist-angle variation should count as a maturity defect for a 2026 prize, or only matter if the citation claimed a mechanism.

Whether the omission of Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, is judged an unrepaired credit gap by the committee; I have not verified how the individual contributions were split inside Jarillo-Herrero's group.

Whether the magic-wavelength lattice is accepted as a distinct step from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have moved toward yes, but this is a judgement on a field far from mine and I have not verified priority among Katori, Ye and other lattice-clock groups.
Whether quantum simulation in B046 counts as a discovery under the prize criterion and whether three names can be chosen without a decisive injustice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B022, B036 or B046: none of the credited candidates are among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutional connections. My interest in statistical physics of complex systems gave me an affinity for B034, which I no longer advance. I note Kroll's disclosure on B036 and Olsson's on B021 and leave those recusal judgements to the committee.
